headline: Jim Copenhaver, shot at Butler in 2024, has died at 76.
summary: Jim Copenhaver was in the bleachers in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a gunman fired at Trump in 2024. One bullet grazed Trump's ear. Two hit Copenhaver in the arm and the abdomen. He walked with a cane after. He died Wednesday in a Pittsburgh hospital, his lawyer said. He and his wife sued the government in June over security that day.

cover_question.q: Did the bullet make him die?

cover_answer: Pennsylvania's attorney general says yes, two years on.
table_question: If harm shows up two years late, who still owes for it?

5-7.script: Two years ago a man fired a gun at a big outdoor rally where Trump was speaking. A man named Jim in the stands was hit and never got all the way better. He died this week. He was 76, about as old as a great-grandpa. That was far from here, and the man with the gun was stopped that same day. You're safe.
5-7.why: Hit, then not all the way better, then gone: one line a seven-year-old can hold. The gun stays two years back, and stopped.
5-7.why_long: A seven-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script keeps the gun two years back and stopped, and puts a man who never got all the way better in front. Great-grandpa's age is the anchor. Expect "could that happen to you?" No. That was one rally, far from here, and it is over.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: In 2024 a gunman on a rooftop fired at a Trump rally. Jim Copenhaver was hit twice; a bullet stayed near his spine. He died Wednesday. Security is a checklist: who's on the roof, who watches the crowd. His family says a step was skipped.
8-12.why: A rooftop, two bullets, two years. The checklist is the lawsuit.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether adults did their jobs, so the script hands them a chain with a gap in it: rooftop, two bullets, surgeries, two years, then Wednesday. The checklist, a mechanism they trust from fire drills, turns a lawsuit into who skipped a step. Expect "did the Secret Service get in trouble?" Not yet. The suit is from June.

13-17.script: If a man dies two years after being shot, did the gunman kill him? Pennsylvania's attorney general says the wounds did. No court will say: the gunman died that day. Second: Copenhaver sued the Secret Service in June. When protection fails, who owes what?
13-17.why: Two questions with no clean answer. Let them pick the harder one.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things: the gunman was killed that day, and the state says his bullets killed a second man two years later. The script gives them that count, then a harder one: can a family bill the Secret Service for the roof nobody watched? Expect "was it really the wounds?" His family did not say. The state did.

5-7.q: Did the bullet make him die?
5-7.a: Pennsylvania's top lawyer says yes, from the wounds. It was two years ago and far from here. You're safe.

8-12.q: Why did he die now and not then?
8-12.a: Shot in the arm and the belly, many surgeries, a bullet near his spine. The state says complications from those wounds.
The gunman was killed that day. Copenhaver and his wife sued the government in June, saying security failed.

13-17.q: Does this count as the gunman's second killing?
13-17.a: Pennsylvania's attorney general says complications from his wounds. Corey Comperatore died that day. No court will rule.

13-17.q: Can a family sue the Secret Service?
13-17.a: He and his wife did in June, saying it "utterly failed" to secure the rally. David Dutch, also shot, sued too.
